# How much improvement from replacing an O2 sensor?

When you are staring at a fuel economy gap like yours—getting 19.6 mpg in city driving on a vehicle that should be hitting around 26 mpg—the instinct is to replace parts until the needle moves. You recently tackled plugs, filters, and even swapped out the coolant temperature sensor because it was reading high, which explains why mileage jumped from roughly 10 mpg back up to nearly 20. That was a smart diagnostic step; the ECU relies heavily on that upstream sensor data to manage idle and warm-up enrichment cycles. However, if no error codes appeared after pulling the scanner, you are likely dealing with a "lazy" failure rather than a catastrophic one.

The oxygen sensor (O2) is essentially the feedback loop for your engine's air-fuel ratio. In a wideband system or even a standard narrowband setup found in your 1997 Mazda Protegé, the sensor tells the Powertrain Control Module (PCM) whether the mixture is lean (too much air) or rich (too much fuel). If the sensor is sluggish—unable to switch voltage states quickly from 0.1V to 0.9V—the PCM defaults to a slightly richer mixture just to be safe. This "rich bias" prevents engine knock but burns extra gasoline. The absence of a trouble code like P0130 or P0135 doesn't guarantee the sensor is performing within spec; it only means the voltage hasn't crossed specific thresholds that trigger a failure flag during the drive cycle.

To quantify whether replacing the sensor will yield results, you need to look at data logs, not just the check engine light. Modern OBD-II scanners can display live data streams showing the "O2 Sensor Status" or "Fuel Trim." Look for the Long Term Fuel Trim (LTFT) and Short Term Fuel Trim (STFT) percentages while driving in steady city traffic. If your LTFT is sitting at +8% to +15%, it indicates the PCM is actively adding fuel because it perceives a lean condition, often due to sensor lag or contamination. A healthy system should hover near 0% when warm and cruising.

If you don't have an advanced scanner, there is a manual test you can perform with a digital multimeter. Disconnect the O2 sensor connector and back-probe the signal wire (usually the white/red pair). Ground your meter's negative lead to the engine block. The voltage should fluctuate rapidly between roughly 0.1V and 0.9V whenever the throttle is applied or RPMs change. If the voltage sits stuck around 0.45V, drifts very slowly, or takes minutes to switch after a cold start, the sensor is degraded. A sluggish sensor causes the PCM to enrich the mixture unnecessarily, directly contributing to that missing 6 mpg.

However, there are diminishing returns to consider. Even if you install a brand-new Bosch Zexel unit tomorrow, your mileage might only jump from 19.6 to 21 or 22 mpg if other factors—such as ignition timing, exhaust leaks, or tire pressure—are also pulling efficiency down. In your case, since the coolant sensor was faulty, ensuring that new sensor is calibrated correctly is critical before blaming the O2 sensor again.

For developers and engineers who appreciate how this logic translates to code, think of the ECU as a PID controller trying to maintain a target value (14.7:1 air-fuel ratio). The O2 sensor provides the error signal (`error = measured - target`). If the sensor response time increases, the integral term in that loop accumulates, causing the actuator (fuel injector pulse width) to overshoot and sustain higher consumption until the system re-stabilizes, which it never fully does if the input is noisy.

Given your mileage gap and the lack of error codes, I recommend logging live fuel trims for a weekend drive before buying another part. If those numbers are elevated, a replacement will likely provide a modest but real gain, perhaps 1 to 3 mpg depending on how severe the sensor lag is.
